at.step: Reveal: the plant floor is segmented on purpose

at.step: Reveal: the plant floor is segmented on purpose

items.item: ISA's own standards pages prohibit AI-tool ingestion of their content; the series is named bibliographically only and not fetched or quoted

A network-segmentation model and a data-ownership model answer different questions that look like the same question: segmentation says which wire a packet may cross, ownership says which team's word is final about what a byte on either side of that wire means.

at.step: Reveal: the plant floor is segmented on purpose

items.item: A read that never writes can still be destructive, because the scarce resource a controller protects isn't just its memory, it's its own scan loop's time budget — the same budget its control logic depends on to run at all.

at.step: Predict: can a read-only script still disturb control?

items.item: A load budget computed before deployment is the cheapest form of this check there is: multiplying a tag count by a poll rate takes a sentence, and it would have caught the hook's conveyor fault before a single request left the laptop.

at.step: Reveal: the load budget, computed

items.item: Subscribing instead of polling is the textbook fix taught in isolation from any actual budget, and the moment you attach a real number to it, it stops being obviously sufficient — a half-fix that still breaches the budget is a worse trap than an obviously-wrong naive poll, because it looks solved.

at.step: Reveal: a subscription is better, and still not enough

items.item: The right fix isn't a smaller ask of the same system, it's asking a different system that was already built to carry that kind of load as part of its own job — a historian already absorbs the change-of-value firehose for its own archival purpose, so a reader against it adds nothing new to the PLC's side of the boundary.

at.step: Reveal: read from the thing built to absorb it

items.item: A buffer that drops its own oldest item under pressure is choosing which side of the boundary pays the cost of a stall — and the one rule that can never be violated is that the producer, which sits closer to the controller, must never be the one asked to wait.

at.step: Reveal: a slow consumer can't block the producer

items.item: Ownership of a definition and ownership of the bytes that store it are two separate facts that happen to usually travel together — the moment a definition's bytes move to a system owned by a different team, that pairing breaks, and a pipeline that assumes it still holds will silently redefine something it never had the authority to redefine.

at.step: Reveal: ownership is assigned, not inferred

items.item: An alias contract is cheap exactly because it does nothing clever — it just keeps a dictionary of every name a thing has ever had, which turns a rename from an event a downstream reader has to survive into an event it never notices.

at.step: Reveal: a rename breaks the naive reader, not the contract reader

items.item: A subscription against a PLC's own OPC UA server is not automatically exempt from the budget question just because it is passive on the wire — the PLC still does the work of deciding what counts as a change, so the same arithmetic that broke the naive poll applies to it, only with a different multiplier.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Naming a cross-chapter concept id without checking it exists in registry.ts yet is its own failure mode, distinct from any technical bug: a plan that says a topic 'builds on Ch.N' is only as reliable as the check that Ch.N's topic actually shipped before this one did — this topic's own Chapter 10/11 gap is an example of exactly that check being run and failing honestly, rather than skipped.
